guide.title: Documentation & the Patient Care Report
guide.lead: Your report is the only lasting record of what you found and did. Write it soon, write what you saw rather than what you think, and never write anything that didn't happen. If it wasn't documented, it wasn't done.

sections.title: Why it matters
items: Continuity of care: the hospital reads it
Legal record: it may be read in court years later
Billing
Research and system data
Quality improvement

sections.title: Narrative formats
rows: Subjective (the patient's words), Objective (your findings), Assessment (your impression), Plan (treatment and transport)
Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx (treatment), Transport
Events in time order: useful for long or complex calls

sections.title: Describe, don't judge
rows: "Slurred speech, unsteady gait, smell of alcohol on breath"
"Struck at the crew twice; restrained with soft limb restraints" – with times
Quote what was said and done

sections.title: Every report
items: Times: call, arrival, patient contact, departure, arrival at hospital
At least two sets of vital signs, with times
Pertinent negatives ("denies chest pain")
Each treatment: time, dose, route, who gave it, response
Who you handed over to
One report per patient

steps.title: Paper
steps.text: One line through the error, initial and date it, write the correct entry. Never erase or use correction fluid.

steps.title: Electronic
steps.text: Add a time-stamped addendum; never delete the original.

steps.title: Late entries
steps.text: Label them as late, with the time written.

groups.title: Refusal
items: Capacity and how you assessed it
Risks explained in their words
Signature or refusal to sign; witness

groups.title: Restraint
items: Why it was needed and what you tried first
Type, time on and off
Regular checks of breathing, circulation and limbs

groups.title: Never
items: Make up or estimate missing vital signs
Record care that wasn't given
Combine patients on one report

quiz.q: Which is NOT a function of the patient care report?
A report is subpoenaed. Which principle applies?
options: If it wasn't documented, it wasn't done
Minor details can be left out
Reports can't be used in court
quiz.explanation: Write it as if a court will read it.

quiz.q: Correcting an error on a paper report:
options: One line through it, initial and date it
Rewrite the whole report and throw away the original

quiz.q: Capable patient refuses after a minor fall. Most important to document:
options: That they understood the risks and had capacity
Your opinion that they needed transport
quiz.explanation: Plus their signature or refusal to sign.

options: "Slurred speech and a strong smell of alcohol on his breath"
quiz.explanation: Describe what you saw, heard and smelled.

options: They write the narrative for you
They can't be used in court

quiz.q: When should you complete the report?
options: As soon as possible after the call, ideally before the next one
Why, what type, how long, and repeated checks of breathing and circulation
quiz.explanation: Restraint can kill; the record must show you monitored.
Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx, Transport.

quiz.q: A colleague wants to record a treatment that wasn't given 'because it looks better'. You:
options: Refuse: falsifying a report is illegal and unethical
Record it if they were busy

flashcards.question: PCR
flashcards.answer: Patient care report: the legal and clinical record of the call.

flashcards.question: The documentation rule
flashcards.answer: If it wasn't documented, it wasn't done.

flashcards.question: SOAP
flashcards.answer: Subjective (the patient's words), Objective (your findings), Assessment (your impression), Plan (treatment and transport).

flashcards.question: Correcting a paper report
flashcards.answer: One line through the error, initial and date, then the correct entry. Never erase. Electronic: time-stamped addendum.

flashcards.question: Five functions of the report
flashcards.answer: Continuity of care, legal record, billing, research, quality improvement.

flashcards.question: CHART
flashcards.answer: Chief complaint, History, Assessment, Rx (treatment), Transport.

flashcards.question: Documenting a refusal
flashcards.answer: Capacity and how you checked it, risks explained, alternatives offered, their words, signature or refusal to sign, witness, medical direction contact.

flashcards.question: Why objective language
flashcards.answer: Judgemental words are unprofessional, often wrong, and damaging in court. Describe what you saw, heard and smelled; quote the patient.

critical.scenario: Inferior STEMI call: you gave oxygen, aspirin and nitroglycerin; pain 8/10 to 4/10. Back at base your partner can't remember the en-route vital signs and says 'I'll make up something close'.
critical.question: Correct course?

options.t: Record only the values you're sure of, note that en-route vital signs weren't recorded, talk to your partner, and report it if they insist

critical.explanation: Monitors often store vital signs: check the device memory.

critical.scenario: A capable driver with neck pain refused a collar and transport and signed. Two days later she's diagnosed with a C5 fracture. Your supervisor reviews your report.
critical.question: What will defend your care best?

options.t: Detailed mental status, neuro findings, the specific risks you explained, her signature and a witness

options.f: Too thin to show an informed refusal.

critical.explanation: Specifics show the refusal was informed.

critical.scenario: Three patients from one crash: a child with a scalp cut, a man with chest pain from the airbag, an older woman with hip pain. A colleague suggests one report for all three.
critical.question: Best response?

options.t: A separate report for each patient, with the right findings and care matched to each

critical.kpi: Completes separate reports for multiple patients
